newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mudslide kills 19 in southern Japan.
newsitem.headline: Mudslide kills 19 in southern Japan.

text.p: Tons of mud and rocks swept over this sleeping village in southern Japan on Thursday, killing 19 people when the side of a mountain loosened by recent earthquakes collapsed in torrential rain.
Two residents of this orange-growing village also were missing and 15 were in hospital after a fearsome midnight landslide buried homes roof-high in mud, rocks and trees.
Nearly 1,000 rescuers, including soldiers, dug with bare hands through debris in the village in Kagoshima Prefecture on southern Kyushu island, 985 km (615 miles) southwest of Tokyo.
"I've never seen such a disaster," Kagoshima governor Tatsuro Suga said from the place where the village once stood.
With rain still falling, it is buried under an estimated 100,000 cubic metres (130,800 cubic yards) of debris, a volume that rescue workers said would fill 16,000 large trucks.
Triggered by four days of torrential rain, the side of a hill overlooking the village crumbled without warning and sank into the narrow Harihara river shortly after midnight.
The huge wall of mud and rocks spewed along the river bed, flowing over and through a partially constructed 14 metre (43 ft) high landslide-barrier built to prevent such a disaster.

"I heard the ground roar and I quickly looked outside the door," said one middle-aged housewife of Harihara village, now in hospital. "Then I realised that my neighbour's house was not there...and the one next to it. I was terrified."
Sixteen wooden houses in the village of 80 families were smashed to pieces by the wall of mud, five metre (yard) wide boulders and trees uprooted in the slide down the hill.
Muneyuki Mutagami, a prefectural official in charge of building the barrier, said the landslide was the biggest he had ever seen.

"I have been engaged in work on disaster prevention for 30 years, but I have not seen a landslide bigger than this. It's an avalanche of a mountain hitting the village rather than a landslide," he said.
Mutagami said a series of earthquakes that have jolted the region since last March, coupled with the torrential rain, made the area prone to landslides.
Last month the area was shaken by two strong earthquakes after a number of smaller tremors since the start of the year.
Another landslide on Wednesday night in neighbouring Kumamoto Prefecture buried nine people under mud, but they were all rescued, police said.
Last December, 20 people died in another landslide in Kagoshima Prefecture.
Japan's Meteorological Agency said a powerful front had dumped 800 millimetres (32 inches) of rain since Sunday, one-third of the area's normal rainfall for an entire year.

In other parts of Kyushu, the rain storm damaged 16 homes, flooded more than 600 houses, triggered 180 small landslides and damaged roads in 29 places, police said. Three people were injured in these incidents.

Weathermen said the front could dump another 200 millimetres (7.8 inches) of rain in parts of Kyushu in the next 24 hours, and issued torrential rain and flood warnings over Kyushu and in the western areas of Japan's main island Honshu.
